chapter: Leaving New York, jazz styles and religion
title: New styles came from the West, East copied
summary: Smith says new jazz styles like Kansas City jump came from Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas, where players had individual styles, while eastern arrangers copied.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Do you think, though, to any extent at all that this very competitive attitude among musicians is one of the things that made Jazz advance musically very fast? Do you think that it actually helped the music? It was bad for the musicians, but do you think it was good for the music?

Well, in a way... I'll tell you what. They can say what they want. But mostly when them styles change, it's mostly back West somewhere. Like Kansas City come up with that different kind of jump. And most of the musicians, it comes back out West here. Like, Charlie Parker came in there with that new way of playing. Yeah, all right. And if they like it, some of them Eastern musicians, if they like it, they'll pick up on it. Johnny Hodges. Johnny Hodges came in with all that beautiful playing and that big tone and everything, and he had a lot of cats trying to copy behind him. Tab Smith loved him. He tried to play just like him.
Yeah. And there's solos that he played that I

liked, and I copied a lot of them off. I liked them and copied right behind. But most all of that jump stuff, with the different kind of Jazz and Blues, Rhythm-and-Blues stuff, most of it comes from out West -- in the middle of the country, like Missouri and Oklahoma, Texas down here. There happen to be quite a few musicians come out of Houston. Yes. Tenor players, all them boys down there.

How do you account for the fact...? Why was it that the Midwest produced something new? What was different about it? What was the difference between the kind of jump rhythm and the stuff they'd been playing out East before that?
Well, we all (?). It looked like there's more individuals. The guy had his own individual style.

Yeah, out West. And each musician, like that tenor player around here, you never heard of him, of the name Earvin(?) Davis. He played a devil of a lot of tenor. But he wouldn't go East. He went to California. I ain't heard of him in years and years. I don't know whether he's still living or not. But anyway, everybody had a different style. And he didn't try to copy up to the other fellows.
Almost all of those musicians in New York, especially those arrangers, they all tried to arrange alike. In other words, they copied on arrangements and arranged alike. Fletcher Henderson

was about the onliest one that was about a little bit different, and of course Duke, he was a little bit different, too. They had a lot of weird... It was weird the way they'd voice the instrument and make it sound surprising(?).

But all them horn player and things they tried to play a lot, copying up to each other. And most of the other boys, like Hershel Evans and Dick Wilson and Lester Young and all of them out there, they were out West -- they had their own style. And they stayed with it. And they'd make up their own... .They couldn't write no music, but they'd make up their own arrangements, head arrangements, and teach the other guys where they wanted to play.
